Pricing & Discount Strategy Analysis

This section examines whether deeper discounts correlate with higher customer satisfaction or simply increase review volume, and how pricing segments affect outcomes.

Key Finding: Discount-Rating Correlation
Pearson r = -0.156 (p = 0.0000), Spearman ρ = -0.146 (p = 0.0000).
The relationship between discount depth and customer rating is weak and negative. This means discounts are a modest driver of customer satisfaction.

Discount-Review Volume Correlation
Pearson r = -0.106 (p = 0.0000).
The relationship between discount depth and review volume is weak and negative. Discounts do not significantly increase customer engagement as measured by review volume.

Review Sentiment Snapshot

High-level qualitative overview of customer review themes based on keyword frequency analysis across 12,154 review titles and review content.

Sentiment Ratio: Positive-to-negative keyword ratio = 7.1:1
The review corpus is overwhelmingly positive. The most frequent positive themes center on value for money and product quality, while negative themes focus on durability issues and product defects.

Strategic Recommendations

1. Reallocate Discount Spend Toward Product Quality

The Pearson correlation between discount depth and customer rating is r = -0.156 — a weak negative relationship. This confirms that deeper discounts do not produce higher satisfaction. Of products with ≥60% discounts, 22 (4.4%) are rated below 3.5, indicating margin erosion without quality payoff.

Action: Cap discount depth at 40-50% for products rated below 3.5; redirect savings into product quality improvements or curated assortment upgrades.

2. Audit High-Discount, Low-Rating Categories

The following categories show above-average discounting but below-average ratings: Car&Motorbike (avg discount: 42%, avg rating: 3.80), MusicalInstruments (avg discount: 46%, avg rating: 3.90). Heavy discounting here suggests an attempt to compensate for perceived low value.

Action: Conduct quality audits on products in these categories. Consider delisting consistently low-rated SKUs rather than discounting further.

3. Leverage High-Rating, Low-Discount Categories as Growth Engines

Categories that achieve strong ratings with modest discounting represent the highest margin opportunities: OfficeProducts (avg discount: 12%, avg rating: 4.31), Toys&Games (avg discount: 0%, avg rating: 4.30). These categories have earned customer trust without aggressive pricing.

Action: Increase visibility and marketing investment for these categories. Small, targeted promotions can drive volume without significant margin sacrifice.

4. Improve Catalog Quality: Address the 24.2% of Products Rated Below 4.0

Currently, 75.8% of products achieve a rating of 4.0 or above, meaning nearly 24.2% fall below this threshold. Low-rated products drag down category-level trust and increase return rates.

Action: Implement a minimum quality gate (rating ≥ 3.5 within 90 days) for continued listing. Prioritize improvement or replacement of products in the 3.0-3.5 bracket, which are closest to viability.

5. Use Engagement Data to Identify Hidden Gems and Dead Weight

The median rating count is 5,179, but the distribution is heavily right-skewed — a small number of products accumulate the majority of reviews. Products with high ratings but low review counts may be undiscovered winners; those with low ratings and low engagement are candidates for delisting.

Action: Create a two-axis prioritization matrix (rating × engagement) to surface high-potential, underexposed products for promotional uplift and to flag low-engagement, low-rating products for removal.
